newsitem.title: UK: Emerging/developed mkt correlations changing - MSCI.
newsitem.headline: Emerging/developed mkt correlations changing - MSCI.

text.p: Correlations between emerging and developed equity markets which many investors use to calculate risk/return ratios, have become more region-specific in the last three years, according to research from Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI).

MSCI's monthly Newswatch newsletter said MSCI, which started collecting data on emerging markets in December 1987, has been tracking correlations for two periods -- from January 1, 1988 to December 31, 1992 and from January 1, 1993 to June 30, 1996.
From the first to the second period the correlation between the MSCI EMF (Emerging Markets Free index) and the MSCI World Indices "remained relatively stable at approximately 46 percent", MSCI said.
"However, correlation between EMF Latin America and MSCI World rose from 27 percent to 33 percent, while that between MSCI EMF Asia and the MSCI World fell from 53 percent to 38 percent."

A lower correlation means that the different markets are more out of step with each other and therefore provide the investor with a better diversification prospect. MSCI compared its developed market indices (like MSCI World) with its various emerging market indices (like MSCI EMF).
"Within regions, there is a notable change in correlations between developed and emerging markets," MSCI added in the note.
"The U.S. and Latin American markets are more closely correlated now than before (31 percent in the later period against 23 percent earlier), although the correlation is still quite low.
But Asian emerging markets have diverged from Japan "to a remarkable degree", with correlation dropping to nine percent from 35 percent.
"This indicates emerging market correlations could be region-specific, and certain emerging markets may be better than others for diversifying investments in particular developed markets."

According to "efficient frontier" theory widely adopted by international fund managers, some investment in low-correlation emerging markets actually reduces the overall risk profile of a global portfolio, while increasing its total returns.

The MSCI U.S. index had a lower correlation with the MSCI EMF in the 1993-1996 period than in 1988-92, dropping from 40 percent to 33 percent. Similarly the correlation between the MSCI Japan and MSCI EMF indices plunged from 33 percent to 15 percent.

MSCI expressed surprise that correlations between the U.K. market and emerging market indices had risen, and attributed it to higher correlation (up to 32 percent from 10 percent) between the U.K. and the Latin American indices.
Despite the changing profile of correlations, MSCI said global portfolio investors should still buy emerging markets.

From inception in 1988 through to mid-1996, the MSCI EMF Index returned (in dollar terms with gross dividends reinvested) over 500 percent, compared with the MSCI's U.S. index return of 262 percent and the EAFE (Europe, Australasia and Far East) of just 82 percent.
